Passengers have criticised the Federal Government’s plan to make the National Identification Number compulsory for domestic air travel from 1 January, 2027, questioning the rationale behind the policy and its implications for foreigners and Nigerians without NIN. On Monday, while announcing the introduction of the Verified Passenger Access System, a biometric facial recognition system designed for domestic air travel across Nigeria and which mandatorily requires a National Identification Numbers, the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, insisted that all airlines must comply with the directive. The proposed policy, Keyamo said, was part of plans to strengthen airport security and improve passenger identification, but the development has been met with concerns over data protection, freedom of movement and the possible exclusion of travellers who rely on other valid means of identification. On Monday, many passengers at Lagos airport condemned the planned introduction of the requirement for local flights, describing it as unnecessary and questioning how it would address the country’s security challenges. A mother of three, Mrs Juliet Adeoye, questioned how the policy would affect foreigners and Nigerians whose children hold citizenship of other countries. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources She questioned the policy, saying two of her children held foreign citizenship and asking whether they would be barred from domestic flights from January for not having NIN, likening the requirement to demanding a UK National Insurance number to book a domestic flight. “I have been wondering where this is coming from since I read the news yesterday, but I strongly hope they will have a rethink before the set date.” Another passenger, Mr Kelvin Jones, commended the government’s intention to improve security but questioned the decision to make NIN a requirement for domestic flight bookings. The concerns have also spilled onto social media, where Nigerians have questioned how the proposed verification system would accommodate foreign passengers and protect travellers’ personal information. Speaking through their X handles, Adesina Adegbite, with the handle @fatiscoproduct, asked how foreign travellers using domestic airports would be verified under the proposed arrangement. He said, “How will the foreigners travelling through the domestic airports passes through the NIN verification system ? What means of identification would be used to verify them?” Similarly, another X user, Ademax, with the handle @Ademaxworld, described the NIN requirement as unnecessary, arguing that other measures could be adopted to address identity fraud and ticketing irregularities. He said, “You don’t need our equivalent of social security numbers to fly domestically in Nigeria. Saying it’s to tackle fake identities and ticketing racketeering is ridiculous as ther should be other ways of doing that without further exposing passengers NIN to hackers!.” Another user, Hon Jay, with the handle @Zellencekelly, acknowledged the importance of airport security but warned against making NIN the only acceptable means of identification for domestic air travellers. He said, “Improving airport security is commendable, but making NIN the sole requirement for domestic flights unfairly excludes Nigerians with other valid means of identification. Security should not become a barrier to citizens’ freedom of movement.” The controversy followed the Federal Government’s announcement of a new passenger verification system, known as VPASS, which will link travellers’ identities to their National Identification Numbers. When contacted, spokesperson of the Airlines Association of Nigeria, Prof. Obiora Okonkwo, said the association has no reaction to the develolopment. He said “We have no reaction.” Olasunkanmi Akinlotan Akinlotan is a journalist at Punch Newspapers with over eight years of experience reporting on politics, social justice, motoring, railways, and aviation.
